transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Stokes (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (CTO, HelioGrid), Priya Nambiar (ML Lead), Luis Ortega (Platform), Samira (Privacy), Tom (Procurement)

Summary:
High-level discovery focused on migration risk and portability from current OpenAI-hosted stack to Redwood. Key drivers: cost predictability (token costs have spiked), latency for multi-region users, and data residency / KMS requirements for EU/US customers. Team is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) options with a likely pilot on hosted/Dedicated before private. Want to validate eval parity (TGI/vLLM models) and run a short perf pilot with their prompts.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and painpoints (OpenAI + some vLLM locally for dev)
- Need for predictable SLA and cheaper per-token unit economics at scale
- Private deployment requirements: KMS, audit logs, SSO, and data residency for EU customers
- Model compatibility: running same model flavors (llama-like, Mistral?) on Redwood; parity with vLLM/TGI and output consistency vs Anthropic/OpenAI
- Benchmarks: latency vs cost trade-off, batch sizing, and KV cache expectations
- Next steps: pricing, security docs, pilot runbook, architecture deep-dive

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, automated transcription with small errors):
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — excited to chat through HelioGrid's migration considerations. Quick intros?
[00:08] Jared: Hi, Jared here, CTO. We run a lot of user-facing summarization/insights, so latency and cost are big for us.
[00:16] Priya: Priya, ML lead. We're doing most production on OpenAI right now, but we run local dev on vLLM for some tests.
[00:23] Luis: Luis — infra/platform, I'll be owning the networking side.
[00:27] Tom: Tom in procurement, quick clarifying Qs on license terms later.
[00:31] Maya: Great, thanks. Evan, do you want to kick off on the tech side?
[00:35] Evan: Sure. So high level — Redwood gives hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private VPC/on-prem options. For migrations we typically help with eval parity — make sure your prompt outputs are consistent — and then run a pilot to measure latency and token cost.
[00:50] Priya: Quick question — we use some TGI adapters and a few quantized checkpoints in vLLM, will those run on Redwood exactly the same?
[00:58] Evan: Short answer — we support most common architectures, and we have execution paths tuned for quantized weights. Might not be 100% identical in floating point rounding and some tokenizer differences can show up. We do eval parity runs and can help with mapping. For TGI/vLLM artifacts, we often port the model and run a controlled eval to surface deltas.
[01:20] Priya: Okay, so we should expect to run tests to compare outputs?
[01:23] Evan: Yeah, we recommend a small prompt set — maybe 500 prompts — and we run diff stats and quality checks.
[01:30] Jared: Our legal/privacy team cares about KMS and audit logs cause we process EU PII. Samira is here — any immediate red flags?
[01:38] Samira: We need customer-managed KMS, at-rest encryption with HSM-backed keys if possible, and retention settings. Also, where logs live is important — cannot have raw prompt copies landing in third-party analytic stores.
[01:50] Maya: That's totally reasonable. Redwood Private offers customer KMS integrations and audit logs; hosted can also be configured with higher controls but Dedicated/Private gives stronger isolation. We'll send the security brief with SOC2/ISO statements and KMS patterns.
[02:03] Tom: And pricing — how does cost look versus OpenAI per token? We're seeing variability month-to-month and want predictability.
[02:12] Maya: For hosted, it's usage-based similar to what you see now but with our model mix optimized for unit-cost. Dedicated gives fixed committed capacity which usually lowers per-token cost for steady workloads; Private is a license + infra model. We'll send a comparison sheet.
[02:27] Luis: On networking — our infra wants VPC peering and SAML SSO. Does Redwood support SAML and fine-grained RBAC?
[02:35] Evan: Yes — we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and VPC peering for Private and Dedicated. Hosted supports SSO and enterprise network options but peering is a Private feature. We can also scope a transit-only approach if you want limited egress.
[02:49] Priya: For the eval parity — we use several prompt templates that rely on subtle tokenization behavior. If the tokenizers differ, can that break our scoring?
[02:59] Evan: It can. The plan is to include tokenizer checks as part of the pilot. We run a tokenizer alignment pass and then the output comparison — we report TTR and token-level diffs. In practice, many customers see small deltas but functionally equivalent outputs after minor prompt tuning.
[03:18] Jared: Any customers who've ported from OpenAI and kept the same product SLAs?
[03:23] Maya: Yes, we've had a few fintech/health customers do hosted->dedicated transitions; Redwood's rollouts and automatic fallback policies helped them maintain availability during cutover. We can share a short case study.
[03:34] Samira: Data residency — our EU clients require prompt payloads never leave EU regions. Can you host model inference entirely in eu-west?
[03:42] Evan: We do regional routing and can keep traffic in EU regions for Private and for Dedicated in supported regions. Hosted can be regionally constrained too depending on model availability; we'll map that in the architecture deep-dive.
[03:56] Tom: If we do a pilot, what does it look like? Timeboxed?
[04:00] Evan: Typically 3-5 days for a perf+parity run: ingest sample prompts, run a batch comparison for outputs, run latency p95/p99, and cost projection with your traffic profile. We can also do a small A/B to validate user-facing metrics.
[04:13] Priya: For models — we use OpenAI's gpt-4-ish for certain workflows and Mistral-like models for others. Do you have equivalent models or do we need to re-run evals on different model families?
[04:24] Evan: We have a model catalog of curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles. For closed models we don't host proprietary OpenAI weights, so parity means either running comparable open models or using redwood-hosted compatible variants. That is a tradeoff; we'll quantify quality delta in the pilot.
[04:40] Jared: Hmm, that quality delta is the business risk. If we see regression on key prompts, what's the rollback path?
[04:46] Maya: We usually recommend canary rollouts with automatic fallback to the prior provider or alternate model variant. Redwood's routing policy can failover to another region/tier. For critical flows you can keep a shadow call to your current provider during the pilot.
[04:59] Luis: Operationally — how does KV cache and batching behavior compare? We rely on prefix caching to save cost.
[05:05] Evan: We have automatic KV cache and continuous batching; configuration will affect latency vs cost. We'll propose batch window settings and caching TTLs in the runbook. Some transcription notes: when customers moved from self-hosted vLLM to Redwood, they tuned batch windows to maintain p95.
[05:22] Priya: Any gotchas with quantized checkpoints when moving from vLLM to your runtime?
[05:27] Evan: Good question — quantization can interact with kernel selection; we may need to re-quantize or re-export the checkpoint. We try to preserve behavior but sometimes need a small retrain or prompt tweaks. We log any artifacts and diff metrics.
[05:40] Jared: Security — Samira asked about logs not leaving. Can logs be stored in our S3 and not in any Redwood analytics bucket?
[05:47] Maya: We can stream logs to customer-owned buckets for Private and Dedicated. For hosted, we offer a similar option under enterprise plans. We'll note that in the security brief.
[05:58] Tom: About contract length — if we do Dedicated reserve, what's typical commitment?
[06:02] Maya: Standard is monthly or annual commits; annual gives better discounts. For pilot we often do a short-term reserved node or a pilot SKU.
[06:12] Priya: For the pilot prompts, we have a set that stresses hallucination/chain-of-thought. Can Redwood instrument quality metrics beyond simple BLEU/perplexity?
[06:21] Evan: Yes — we can run custom evals and provide precision/recall on targeted QA prompts, hallucination rates, and semantic similarity metrics. We can also hook into your existing evaluation harness if you share it.
[06:34] Jared: Are there known differences when using Anthropic-style safety layers vs OpenAI?
[06:40] Evan: Our platform supports safety wrappers and policy layers; if you're using Anthropic-specific safety behavior you may need to re-evaluate policy mappings. We'll help map those in the quality checks.
[06:53] Samira: For compliance, we need vendor attestations and a runbook for incident response.
[06:58] Maya: We'll include SOC2/ISO summaries and an incident response template. Also can include details on data deletion and retention controls.
[07:10] Luis: Quick infra Q — do you support private subnets and restricted egress for customer model containers?
[07:16] Evan: Yes for Private/on-prem. For Dedicated we can work with cloud provider networking to limit egress. We'll document network topology options in the architecture session.
[07:27] Priya: For the tokenizer differences — is it feasible to keep using our current tokenization pipeline?
[07:32] Evan: You can. If you serve tokenization before the request and ensure consistent handling, that'll reduce differences. We'll validate that in the tokenizer alignment step.
[07:44] Jared: Budget — if we run a pilot and it looks good, what's a typical ramp plan?
[07:49] Maya: Many customers start with non-critical flows, then expand. Typical cadence: pilot -> staged traffic shift -> full cutover over 4-12 weeks depending on risk.
[07:58] Tom: Procurement will want sample MSA/terms to review.
[08:02] Maya: We'll provide standard terms and a pilot addendum.
[08:06] Evan: For the technical checklist, I'll need your sample prompt corpus, target SLAs, and traffic profile. Priya, can you share that?
[08:14] Priya: Yeah, I'll pull a balanced set and include the evaluation harness. Give me the expected format.
[08:19] Evan: CSV or ndjson with prompt, expected answer, and meta. We'll send a template.
[08:25] Maya: Okay, quick recap of next steps — we'll send security brief + pricing no later than 2026-05-08, SE will send pilot runbook and template by 2026-05-10, and we'll aim to kickoff perf pilot the week of 2026-05-11.
[08:40] Jared: Sounds good. Any other Qs?
[08:44] Tom: No, just to confirm procurement will need a contact for MSA questions.
[08:48] Maya: That's me — I'll loop in legal.
[08:51] Samira: Thanks, this was helpful.
[08:54] Maya: Thank you all — we'll follow up with the docs.

End of meeting.
